why_angle: The cited pages give temperature ratings only for installer batteries: Solar Examiner lists Powerwall 3 at -4–122°F and aPower 2 at -4–131°F. None of them gives the charging-temperature limit or the refill hours for a backup kit you can order. This page adds the Apex 300's 32–104°F charging window (StorageReview) against the outdoor-rated E10's 131°F (Anker), plus the runtime and refill arithmetic.

page.answer: Short answer. The best home battery backup you can order for a Texas home is the Anker SOLIX E10 Automatic Backup Kit: 12.3 kWh and 7,680 W at 240 V, rated to run at up to 131°F outdoors. BLUETTI's cheaper Apex 300 kit only charges between 32°F and 104°F, so it has to stay indoors.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Energy Collective puts a 2-ton central AC at about 3,800 W running and 5,800 W to start, a refrigerator at about 700 W, and a half-horsepower furnace blower at about 800 W. Here's how each kit holds up against those loads, before inverter losses:

  • E10, two batteries: 12.288 kWh ÷ 3.8 kW ≈ 3.2 h of 2-ton AC; 12.288 ÷ 1.5 kW (fridge + blower) ≈ 8.2 h.
  • E10, one battery: 6.144 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 1.6 h of AC; 6.144 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 4.1 h of fridge + blower.
  • BLUETTI Apex 300 + B300K: 5.53 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 1.5 h of AC. At the 89% StorageReview measured with two B300K: 4.92 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 1.3 h. Fridge + blower: 5.53 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 3.7 h.
  • Headroom while the AC runs: 3,840 − 3,800 = 40 W left on the Apex 300; 7,680 − 3,800 = 3,880 W left on the E10.
  • Cost per rated kWh: $7,799 ÷ 12.288 ≈ $635; $4,299 ÷ 6.144 ≈ $700; $3,199 ÷ 5.53 ≈ $579.
Your situationKit

{kit:kit-anker-e10-automatic} is the kit for most Texas homes. It can sit outdoors (IP66) and still run at 131°F, its 7,680 W carries a 2-ton AC with room to spare, and the Power Dock switches the house over without you touching anything. Anker says an electrician has to install the Power Dock.

{kit:kit-anker-e10-inlet} has the same outdoor-rated unit with one 6.144 kWh battery and a manual inlet box. It fits if your outages usually last hours, not days, and you're fine switching over by hand. You can add B6000 batteries later yourself (up to 5 per E10).

{kit:kit-bluetti-apex-300-indoor} is the cheapest kit per kWh and gives 240 V from one unit, but it has to live in conditioned space. It leaves only 40 W of headroom while a 2-ton AC runs, and BLUETTI expects it to ship in late January.

If you're adding rooftop solar through an installer, that's a different purchase. Solar Examiner lists the Powerwall 3 at 13.5 kWh and 11.5 kW, rated -4°F to 122°F, at about $15,000 median installed with solar (Solar.com figure). It lists the FranklinWH aPower 2 at 15 kWh, rated -4°F to 131°F, at about $17,250. Installers quote both; we don't sell them.

The 104°F limit: where the battery can live in a Texas summer

StorageReview's spec table for the BLUETTI Apex 300 gives a charging range of 32°F to 104°F and a discharging range of -4°F to 104°F. Above 104°F it is outside both its charging and its discharging range, and BLUETTI's FAQ says it isn't waterproof. A closed Texas garage, patio or attic in July is the wrong place for it. Put it in a room the house AC keeps cool. Winter matters too: below 32°F it won't charge, so an unheated garage during a freeze is a problem as well.

Anker rates the E10 to operate from -4°F to 131°F, with full-speed charging between 59°F and 131°F. Below 59°F a heating film warms the battery. The power module is NEMA 4 (IP66), and the Power Dock and Smart Inlet Box are NEMA 3R. At the top end that matches the aPower 2's 131°F and beats the Powerwall 3's 122°F (Solar Examiner).

Refill time. StorageReview measured 3.30 kWh from the wall to refill one 2.76 kWh Apex 300 (×1.19). For the 5.53 kWh kit that's 5.53 × 1.19 ≈ 6.6 kWh. On the standard 120 V/15 A cord at 1,800 W, that takes 6.6 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 3.7 h. With the 50 A cable at 3,840 W turbo it takes about 1.7 h. Its two solar ports take 1,200 W each (12–60 V), so 1,000 W of panels need about 6.6 h of full sun at best, and only while the unit stays under 104°F. The E10 charges at 7,680 W from 240 V/32 A, so 12.288 ÷ 7.68 ≈ 1.6 h. It has two 4,500 W solar inputs (30–450 V).

Starting the AC. Anker claims one E10 with two or more batteries delivers 155 LRA, which it says starts a 5-ton central AC. It lists 120 A with one battery. Its page also shows a second surge range (120–175 LRA), so check your compressor's LRA label against the lower figure. BLUETTI lists 7,680 W of 'Lifting Power' without saying whether that is motor-start surge, and StorageReview didn't test central AC. BLUETTI's '12kW bypass powers HVACs' figure is grid power passing through the unit, so it doesn't apply during an outage. With the grid down, the limit is 3,840 W, or 16 A at 240 V.

Not recommended

The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus kits: Anker's own page says '240V output cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC.' If you recharge it from a common 120 V portable generator during a long outage, your 240 V circuits, such as central AC and well pumps, go dark. On 2026-11-14 it was also listed as sold out with no price.
